lead: Design is where a software project stops describing the problem and starts deciding the shape of the solution. The requirements model — use cases, classes, data flow diagrams — goes in; a design model comes out: data structures, architecture, interfaces, components and the hardware they sit on. There is no single correct design, so we choose between candidate designs using quality attributes: maintainability, dependability, security, efficiency, acceptability. Every design decision buys one attribute and costs another, and a good design review names both sides. This chapter gives the process, the attributes, and the five elements of the design model.
prereq: You need Unit 2's functional and non-functional requirements and the analysis models, and Unit 1's view of where design sits in the life cycle — see 3.6 for the class model that feeds data design.

sections.h3: The design process: requirements model in, design model out

blocks.text: Analysis produced a requirements model: what the system must do, written as use cases, class models and data flow diagrams. Design reads that model and writes a design model: how the system will do it. Requirements say "book a seat". Design says which tables hold seats, which service takes the booking, which screen shows the seat map, and which server runs that service.

items: Study the requirements model and mark the parts that force structure — volumes, peaks, external systems, legal rules.
Choose the architecture: the large parts, their responsibilities and their connections.
Design the data: tables, files, keys, indexes and the objects that sit on top of them.
Design the interfaces: module-to-module signatures, and the boundary to the user and to other systems.
Design each component: algorithms, internal data, error handling.
Design deployment: which hardware node runs which component, and how nodes talk.
Review the whole design against the quality attributes, and revise the parts that fail.

blocks.text: Design thinking has grown in layers, not by replacement. Modular design treats a program as functions with clean boundaries. Object-oriented design bundles data and behaviour into classes that hide their internals (3.2). Pattern-based design reuses named solutions such as MVC or observer (3.4). Aspect-oriented design pulls cross-cutting concerns such as logging and security checks out of every module and into one separate unit. Each layer gives the designer one more way to keep change local.

Several designs satisfy the same requirements, so we need a way to compare them. We compare them on quality attributes: the non-functional requirements of Unit 2, made concrete enough to shape a decision. Standards and textbooks use different names for the same ideas — ISO 25010 groups them as functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability; McCall's older factor list splits them into product revision, product transition and product operations. Learn the ideas, not the list.

head: Attribute
One-line meaning
rows: The cost of finding and fixing a fault or adding a feature later.
The system keeps working correctly when things go wrong — availability, reliability, safety.
Data and functions are reachable only by those allowed to reach them.
The work gets done within the time and memory budget on the given hardware.
Users can learn and use it, and the organisation can afford to run it.

blocks.text: Design guidelines sit on top of the attributes: a design should be hierarchical, modular, and made of distinct parts with clear boundaries; it should be traceable back to the requirements model; and it should be describable in a standard notation such as UML. The measurable forms of these guidelines — cohesion and coupling — are in 3.2.

No attribute is free. Encrypting card data buys security and costs response time and key management. Caching the seat map buys performance and costs memory and consistency. Running two copies of a service buys availability and costs money and deployment complexity. A design review therefore asks three questions: which attribute, which decision buys it, and which attribute that decision costs.

sections.h3: The five elements of the design model

items: Data design turns the data objects of the analysis model into tables, files, indexes and keys. It is the hardest element to change once live data exists.
Architectural design decides the large parts and their connectors. Styles such as layered, client-server and pipe-filter are catalogued in 3.3.
Interface design covers two edges: internal signatures between modules, and the external edge — the user interface (3.5) and links to other systems.
Component design goes inside each module: the algorithms, local data and error handling, built with the concepts of 3.2 and drawn in 3.6.
Deployment design maps components onto hardware nodes and says how nodes communicate; 3.8 gives the diagram for it.

blocks.text: The five elements are not produced in a fixed order. A peak-load figure in the requirements may force both the cache (data design) and the second server (deployment design) in the same meeting.

figure.caption: The worked example on one line: 99.9 % availability leaves 0.001 of the year down, which is 8.76 h or about 8 h 46 min. Each attribute is then bought by a named design decision — two copies behind a load balancer, and a cached seat map.

spec.title: 99.9 % available: how much downtime, and what buys it
spec.aria: Flow diagram: 99.9 % availability gives an unavailable fraction of 0.001; a 365-day year is 8760 h, so allowed downtime is 0.001 × 8760 = 8.76 h, which is 525.6 min or about 8 h 46 min; the two design decisions are two copies behind a load balancer and a cached seat map.

examples.question: A ticket-booking site must be available 99.9 % of the year and must carry 40,000 users in the 10 a.m. booking window. (a) Name the two quality attributes. (b) How much downtime does 99.9 % allow in a 365-day year? (c) Give one design decision for each attribute.
steps: (a) Availability over a year is a dependability attribute (reliability in service). Carrying 40,000 users in a fixed window is a performance attribute (scalability and response time).
In minutes: 8.76 × 60 = 525.6 min, that is 8 h 45.6 min, about 8 h 46 min a year.

(c) Availability: run two copies of the booking service behind a load balancer, so one server can fail without stopping bookings. Performance: keep the seat map in a cache and hold the seat lock in memory, so a page view does not hit the database.
examples.answer: Attributes are dependability (availability) and efficiency (performance/scalability); 99.9 % allows 8.76 h of downtime a year, about 8 h 46 min.
examples.check:
unavailable = 0.001
hours_in_year = 365 * 24
downtime_h = unavailable * hours_in_year
downtime_min = downtime_h * 60
print(downtime_h)
print(downtime_min)

traps: Writing quality attributes as a wish list. A full answer names the attribute, the design decision that buys it, and the attribute that decision costs.
Mixing the models: sentences beginning "the system shall ..." belong to requirements, not to a design answer.
Confusing architecture with component design. Architecture is the parts and their connectors; component design is what happens inside one part.
Percentage slips in availability: 99.9 % means 0.001 unavailable, not 0.01. Read the number of nines before multiplying.
Forgetting deployment design. A design that never says which machine runs what is incomplete in any exam that asks for the design model.

quiz.q: Name the five elements of the design model.
quiz.a: Data design, architectural design, interface design, component design, deployment design.

quiz.q: Give one-line meanings of maintainability, dependability, security and efficiency.
quiz.a: Maintainability: cost of fixing a fault or adding a feature later. Dependability: keeps working correctly when things go wrong. Security: only authorised users reach data and functions. Efficiency: meets time and memory budgets on the given hardware.

quiz.q: Why must the design process start from the requirements model?
quiz.a: The requirements model holds the obligations the system must meet — behaviour, volumes, external systems, rules. Design decisions are only correct relative to those obligations, and traceability from design back to requirements is how a reviewer checks that nothing was invented and nothing was dropped.

quiz.q: Two designs both satisfy the same requirements. What decides between them?
quiz.a: Quality attributes. Compare each candidate on maintainability, dependability, security, efficiency and acceptability, and on the cost of each choice. The chosen design buys the attributes that matter most for this product and accepts the attributes it sacrifices.

quiz.q: A service must be available 99.95 % of a 365-day year. How many hours of downtime does that allow?
quiz.a: Unavailable fraction = 0.0005. Hours in year = 365 × 24 = 8760 h. Downtime = 0.0005 × 8760 = 4.38 h, about 4 h 23 min.

quiz.q: A team adds a cache for the seat map to survive the 10 a.m. peak. Which attribute is bought, which are risked, and what design element does the cache belong to?
quiz.a: Buys efficiency (response time, throughput). Risks consistency (a user may see a stale seat) and maintainability (extra code to invalidate the cache). It is a data design decision, with a deployment consequence if the cache is a separate server.

quiz.q: A designer moves all logging and access checks out of every module into one separate unit. Which design evolution is this, and which attribute does it target?
quiz.a: Aspect-oriented design, handling cross-cutting concerns. It targets maintainability, because a change to the logging policy is made in one place instead of in every module.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the quality attributes of a system are now usually written down as short architecture decision records: the decision, the attribute it serves, and the option it rejected. ISO 25010 is the standard vocabulary behind most non-functional requirement checklists, and cloud deployment design has made availability and cost into daily design variables rather than review-time afterthoughts. Search for architecture decision records, ISO 25010 quality model, and aspect-oriented programming to go further.
